title: All things in common (Acts 2:37–47)
hook: teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer, and daily added
tomorrow: a man begs at the temple gate. Peter has no money. now what?

segments.voice: That was a week of turning points: a bought story, a promise on a mountain, an order to wait, a twelfth chosen with one accord, flames and many languages, and a denier who stood up. Yesterday's line: the promise is for you.
screen: `THE PROMISE IS FOR YOU.` → `A WEEK OF TURNING POINTS.`

segments.voice: The group chat after a great retreat usually goes quiet within a week. Acts says this crowd didn't. When Peter finishes, "they were pricked in their heart," and they ask, "Men and brethren, what shall we do?" He tells them to repent and be baptized, and Acts counts about three thousand added that day. Then the real question: did it last? Here's what they actually did: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."
screen: `AFTER THE RETREAT, QUIET.` → `WHAT SHALL WE DO?` → `THEY CONTINUED STEDFASTLY.`

segments.voice: Four things: teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer. Some readers hear the breaking of bread as the Lord's Supper, others as shared meals, some as both. Then the line behind today's title: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." They sold what they owned "and parted them to all men, as every man had need." Not equal shares: need. The last picture is a kitchen table: "breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Meat, in the King James, simply means food. Readers take this page different ways: a pattern to copy, a challenge, a portrait of one bright season. Acts just tells it. One to tell a friend tonight: the Greek word for fellowship here is koinonia, from the same family as the word for common. Sharing a life and sharing a table are one idea. And notice the mood word. Not duty. Gladness, around food, in ordinary houses.
screen: `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYER.` · `ALL THINGS COMMON.` · `NOT EQUAL SHARES: NEED.` · `HOUSE TO HOUSE, AT THE TABLE.` · then, large: `WITH GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Take one slow sip or bite of whatever is near: water, tea, a piece of bread. Taste it all the way through, as if it were shared. Then bring to mind who you'd most like at your table this week, and whose table you'd be glad to sit at.
All things in common. The believers in Acts 2 shared what they had, as anyone had need, and ate together with gladness.
Carry this: with gladness, around ordinary tables, sharing as anyone has need. Another week, done.

fork.setup: you share a fridge with roommates. one buys most of the groceries; another is broke this month. what does Acts 2 point toward?
options: share by need this month, without keeping score.
split every bill exactly equal, every time.
each keeps their own shelf, so it stays fair.
fork.reveal: Acts says they parted things to all men, as every man had need. not equal shares: need, and with gladness.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing. Acts 2:42; the same word family as koina, common, in 2:44.

trapdoor: what you thought: an early commune with a rule about money.
what it means: teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer, shared by need, with gladness.
what a scholar hears: koinonia (2:42) and koina (2:44) are one word family: fellowship and having in common go together.
guess: sharing what you have, as each one needs
owning nothing at all, by strict rule
splitting everything in exactly equal parts
recall: to the end of the age

chat.says: announcement went ok!! now six church families want to bring food. Pop says make it a potluck. thoughts?
options: Yes: everyone brings something and you eat together. Acts: bread with gladness.
Better to cater it, so nobody brings more than anyone else: equal shares.
Skip the food. In Acts the point was doctrine and prayer, not the meals.
chat.meaning: They broke bread from house to house with gladness and shared as every man had need. A table everyone brings to fits Acts 2.

stedfastly.meaning: older spelling of steadfastly: firmly, without giving up

brethren.meaning: older English for brothers; fellow believers

repent.meaning: to turn around: change your mind and your way

notes: Week end and review shape (days 1485–1491): the review names the week; games.recall holds the six carries of days 1485–1490 for the review round. The day's word is still taught, lightly.
'About three thousand' comes straight from Acts 2:41 ('about three thousand souls').
Breaking of bread (Acts 2:42, 46): three readings named (the Lord's Supper, shared meals, both) without ranking.
Baptism and repentance (Acts 2:38) are mentioned, not explained, since churches understand baptism differently.
koinonia (2:42) and koina (2:44) as one word family: a standard lexicon relation, not a preacher's etymology. Confirm.
The hook's line that retreat group chats 'usually go quiet' is about the listener's world, not a claim about any tradition.
Practice kind: taste (the outline's 'share a meal', made doable in two minutes).
